Led end-to-end discovery research to define which gaming features to build and prioritize.
Ethnography (8 sessions, Mumbai & Delhi)  →  cross-functional workshop  →  Kano test (n=150).
2 features shipped: FlexDrop & 36-Month Fluency — now on devices of 500M+ users globally.
— the world's #5 smartphone manufacturer — India is the world's #2 smartphone market and one of the fastest-growing.
A predominantly young user base spending heavy daily time on mobile gaming — confirmed by our user behavior data.
Gaming experience ranked among the top 3 improvement areas in NPS verbatim analysis among young Indian users.
Purchase journey research confirmed it: users perceived fewer gaming features on our phones vs. competitors.
to win young Indian users — and keep them — we needed gaming selling points grounded in real user needs, not feature-matching against competitors.
One Business Question, Two Research Questions
Which gaming features should we prioritize to make our phones more appealing than competitors' to young Indian users — driving purchase intent and long-term loyalty?
How do young Indian users play mobile games in their daily lives: in what contexts, and what unmet needs and pain points emerge?
Which candidate features most increase purchase appeal — and which are must-haves vs. delighters?
Long-term usage was tracked post-launch via feature DAU and NPS monitoring (→ Impact).
Qual to Discover, Quant to Prioritize

our prior understanding of Indian users came mostly from remote surveys and online interviews — we had rarely observed real usage contexts, or the pain points users themselves can't articulate. Since gaming features would evolve over years, we invested in one foundational, in-context study.
Fieldwork in India — 10 days, Mumbai & Delhi
3+ hrs/day (internal standard: 3 hrs = moderate, 5+ hrs = heavy user)
Mix of heavy titles (battle / competitive, e.g., PUBG) and light casual games
Same criteria as qual: young users, 3+ hrs/day gaming, mixed occupations and game types.
So quant results directly validated qual-derived concepts on the same population.
First Overseas Study — Prepared, Not Improvised
This was the team's first overseas study. India was culturally and behaviorally unfamiliar to almost everyone — including me.
1 week of dedicated desk research — PEST analysis, cultural studies, anthropological literature on India → a knowledge framework and initial hypotheses, cross-checked against our internal user data.
A deep pre-departure briefing for all ~10 participating stakeholders — nobody landed in India with an empty mental model.
~10 stakeholders joined the fieldwork — team immersion was a design goal, not a side effect.
THE TRADE-OFF — 2 CITIES VS. TEAM IMMERSION
Bringing ~10 stakeholders into the field meant budget and logistics limited us to Mumbai + Delhi.

trade geographic breadth for organizational alignment depth. Stakeholders experienced user contexts firsthand instead of hearing my retelling — which made later buy-in and execution dramatically easier.
For a foundational first study, depth > breadth.
Spend a Day with a User
Full-day in-context observation, followed by a same-day in-depth interview.

Behaviors anchored the conversation. Instead of asking users to recall in a lab room, we probed moments we had just witnessed — “why did you switch out of the game right then?” — surfacing needs users couldn't articulate unprompted.
thematic coding of field notes & debrief transcripts + per-participant empathy maps, merged by segment (→ next slide).
Spending a day with a college student — a heavy mobile gamer
Two complementary lenses on the same raw data — patterns across users, and depth within each user.
Patterns across users: open codes → two themes → two features
Depth within each user: Says / Thinks / Does / Feels — built same-day in the field
“It Shouldn't Get Slower — Even After 3 Years”
Indian users expect their phones to stay smooth for 3+ years — replacement cycles run notably longer than in most markets.
Which means many gaming pain points emerge late in a phone's life: Android lag compounds over time, and gaming amplifies it.
The underlying need: durability — sustained performance, not day-one performance.
3+ yrs — and it must stay smooth
a long-term fluency commitment — later shipped as
A participant deep in a PUBG match. His girlfriend messages him — but a match runs 30+ minutes and can't be paused. The reply came far too late. (He told us the consequences were serious.)
A student on his 1.5-hour bus ride to campus, wanting to switch fluidly between game, music and chat — and finding it clunky every single time.
FlexDrop — official ColorOS demo (click to watch)
users want to immerse fully in games and stay in control of real life. Gaming is part of their life — not a trap that holds them hostage.
lightweight in-game multitasking — later shipped as
Workshop — run immediately after returning, while immersion was fresh.
~10 stakeholders, each contributing 3–5 ideas grounded in scenes they had personally observed → 25+ ideas.
Technical feasibility · differentiation vs. competitors · relevance to gaming scenarios → 12 concepts.
Each concept presented as an illustrated concept card; fielded online with screening and data-quality checks.
Result: both FlexDrop and 36-Month Fluency were classified as attractive features with the highest appeal scores.
Kano Better–Worse analysis — recreated for illustration; positions reflect relative results
We needed each feature's nature (must-have vs. delighter), not just a ranking — only attractive features differentiate in marketing. Kano's paired questions also kept respondent burden low online.
Flagship selling point of the series; ranked among the top 5 selling points in NPS driver analysis
The feature proved so popular that the engineering team committed to further iteration
Monitored via feature DAU and NPS tracking
Both features shipped globally to a user base of 500M+.
I supported these features end-to-end — hands-on through discovery, coaching through evaluation：
The builders had been in the field — they owned the insights. When research capacity ran thin,
I coached PMs and designers to run usability and A/B tests themselves
, sharing my past project documentation as templates and supporting participant recruitment.
needs discovered with Indian gamers proved universal — multitasking control and long-term smoothness resonated across markets and age groups. A local insight became global features.
PEST, culture, anthropology — before landing. Behavior has roots you must know in advance.
Outsiders notice pain points locals have normalized. Being unfamiliar is an advantage if you use it.
Understand before judging — and treat local colleagues as mentors.
Lightweight remote interviews with young users in Bangalore, Chennai and Hyderabad — test whether the insights hold.
Daily logs of games played, problems hit, switching moments — low-cost longitudinal context a single-day visit can't capture.
Coaching PMs and designers on evaluative testing worked — but enablement scales research, it doesn't replace it. Next time: at least one researcher-led usability round before launch.
Happy to discuss the methodology, the trade-offs, or how I'd approach your team's research questions.
